entries.signature: Date(value) | Date(year, month, day[, hour, minute, second])
entries.description: Two different questions under one name. With ONE argument it CONVERTS what it is given: a string in '20260902104525' or '02.09.2026 10:45:25' form, or a number read as seconds since 1970. With THREE OR MORE it BUILDS a date from calendar parts, which is how a date somebody knows is written. Two arguments are refused: a year and a month with no day is not a date.
entries.syntax_block: Date(value) | Date(year, month, day[, hour, minute, second])
entries.parameters: year — 1..9999; month — 1..12; day — a day that exists in that month of that year; hour, minute, second — optional, midnight when omitted. A part outside its range is refused by name rather than rolled over into the next month.

entries.description: The integer part of a number: the fractional part is truncated, nothing is rounded. `Int(3.9)` is `3`, not `4`; truncation goes towards zero, so `Int(-3.9)` is `-3`. Use `Round` when you want rounding.
entries.parameters: num — a number (or a value convertible to one).
entries.return_descr: Number — the integer part of the argument.
entries.example:
Message(Int(3.9));    // 3
Message(Int(-3.9));   // -3
Message(Round(3.9));  // 4 — rounding, not truncation

entries.description: Prints a message to the message window. The marker parameter, when supported, prefixes a pictogram indicating the message's importance.
entries.parameters:
<String> — message text.
<Marker> — optional severity marker; not implemented in Phase 1 and currently ignored.

entries.description: Tests whether the value is the database NULL - a value that came back from SQL as NULL. Distinct from Undefined, which means no value at all; use IsEmptyValue for that one.
Tests whether the value carries anything meaningful: false for Undefined, for NULL, for an empty string, a zero number, an empty date and an empty reference. The usual guard before using a value.

entries.description: Turns a runtime value into text (JSON). Printing a value answers what it LOOKS like; this answers what it IS MADE OF, so a structure survives being written down: a selection, a record set, a document object, an array. Use it where the value exists - beside the line that built it - to see what is inside it, to store it, to compare two of them, or to send one somewhere. What can be written grows with the types: whatever learns to pack itself is covered the day it does.
entries.parameters: value - any value this configuration can hold.
entries.return_descr: The value as JSON text. Raises when the value cannot travel (IsTransferable) or when no configuration is open - the types a reference names live in the configuration's own registry.

entries.description: Reads text written by SerializeValue back into a runtime value - and, with it, BUILDS a value from JSON that was written by hand or arrived from outside. That is the only way to construct one without script: text in, value out. NOT every writing survives the return trip: the JSON view is a rendering, so a date is an ISO string and some shapes flatten. Where a value has to come back exactly as it left, keep the binary form.
entries.parameters: json - text as SerializeValue writes it.
entries.return_descr: The value the text describes. Raises when the text is not JSON a value can be read from, when it names a type this configuration does not have, or when no configuration is open.
